mcqs.question: What does a suffix array actually store for a string s?
options: The full text of every suffix, sorted alphabetically
The starting index of every suffix of s, ordered so that the suffixes they point to are in alphabetical order
A count of how many times each character appears in s
The lengths of every suffix of s, sorted numerically
mcqs.explanation: The array holds only starting indices into the original string, ordered so the suffixes they reference come out sorted — any suffix can be reconstructed as s[index:] without ever storing the string itself. Storing full suffix text or character counts would defeat the compact, index-only design that makes a suffix array space-efficient.

mcqs.question: Prefix doubling builds a suffix array in O(n log n) instead of the naive O(n² log n). What makes each round faster than a fresh from-scratch comparison?
options: It only sorts half the suffixes each round
It skips suffixes that were already correctly placed in the previous round
Each round reuses the previous round's ranks as an O(1) comparison key instead of comparing raw characters one by one
It uses a hash table instead of sorting at all
mcqs.explanation: By re-ranking suffixes using the ranks computed for half the current prefix length, each round's comparisons become O(1) lookups rather than O(prefix length) character comparisons — that's what collapses the total cost from O(n^2 log n) to O(n log n) across the doubling rounds. It still sorts and considers all n suffixes every round; no suffixes are skipped or hashed away.

mcqs.question: Once a suffix array is built, what is the time complexity of checking whether a pattern of length m occurs anywhere in the string?
options: O(m log n), via binary search over the sorted suffixes
O(n), by scanning the suffix array linearly
O(1), by direct index lookup
O(n log n), rebuilding part of the array for each query
mcqs.explanation: Since the suffix array is sorted, a standard binary search locates the pattern in O(log n) suffix comparisons, each costing up to O(m) — giving O(m log n) per query, with the O(n log n) build cost paid once and amortized across many such searches. A linear scan or full rebuild per query would throw away exactly the benefit the sorted structure provides.

mcqs.question: Why does the LCP array only need to record the longest common prefix between ADJACENT suffixes in sorted order, rather than every pair?
options: Non-adjacent suffixes never share a common prefix
The LCP array is only an approximation and adjacent pairs are simply cheaper to compute
Comparing non-adjacent suffixes would take more than O(n) total time to precompute
Sorting groups similar suffixes together, so the longest shared prefix between any two suffixes is always achieved by some pair of adjacent suffixes in between them
mcqs.explanation: Because sorting places similar suffixes next to each other, the common-prefix relationship between any two suffixes is captured by the minimum LCP value along the adjacent pairs between them — a standard property of sorted strings — so recording only adjacent pairs loses no information needed to answer common-prefix questions. Non-adjacent suffixes absolutely can and do share prefixes; the array just doesn't need to store that redundantly.

mcqs.question: How do you find the longest repeated substring of a string once you have its suffix array and LCP array?
options: Sum every value in the LCP array
Take the maximum value in the LCP array
Take the minimum value in the LCP array
Count how many LCP values are greater than zero
mcqs.explanation: The maximum LCP value marks the pair of adjacent (in sorted order) suffixes sharing the longest prefix — and a shared prefix between two suffixes starting at different positions is exactly a repeated substring. Summing, taking the minimum, or counting nonzero entries don't correspond to this definition.

mcqs.question: Why is a suffix array generally preferred over a suffix tree in practice, despite a suffix tree offering O(m) pattern search versus the array's O(m log n)?
options: Suffix trees cannot represent every suffix of a string, only a subset
Suffix arrays support pattern search but suffix trees do not

A suffix array is compact — just an array of integers — and simpler to build and reason about, while a suffix tree's per-node pointer overhead and construction complexity outweigh its search-time edge for most uses
Suffix trees always require more suffixes than actually exist in the string
mcqs.explanation: The suffix array's plain-integer-array representation is far more cache-friendly and memory-compact than a suffix tree's real pointer-heavy nodes, and building it is comparatively straightforward — which is why it's the default choice even though a suffix tree wins asymptotically on raw search time. Both structures fully represent every suffix and both support pattern search; the trade is memory and implementation complexity, not capability.
